question_text: The word “chocolate” is a generic term used to || describe a variety of foods made from the seeds, or || beans, of the cacao tree. The first people known to || have consumed chocolate were the Aztecs, who || used cacao seeds to brew a bitter, aromatic drink. It || was not until the Mexican expedition of Hernan || Cortes in 1519, however, that Europeans first || learned of cacao. Cortes came to the New World || primarily in search of gold, but his interest was || apparently also piqued by the Aztecs’ peculiar || beverage, for when he returned to Spain, his ship’s || cargo included three chests of cacao beans. It was || from these beans that Europe experienced its first || taste of what seemed a very exotic beverage. The || drink soon became popular among those wealthy || enough to afford it, and over the next century cafes || specializing in chocolate drinks began to spring up || throughout Europe.

It has been known for some time that wolves || live and hunt in hierarchically structured packs, || organized in a kind of “pecking order” similar to || that found in flocks of birds. At the top of the || hierarchy in any wolf pack are the senior males, || dominating the others in all matters of privilege || and leadership. As many as three other distinct || subgroups may exist within a pack: mature wolves || with subordinate status in the hierarchy; || immature wolves (who will not be treated as adults || until their second year); and outcast wolves || rejected by the rest of the pack. Each individual || wolf, moreover, occupies a specific position within || these subgroups, taking precedence over wolves of || lower rank in the selection of food, mates, and || resting places and holding a greater share of the || responsibility for protecting the pack from strange || wolves and other dangers.

The Romantic poets in nineteenth-century || Britain prided themselves on their rejection of || many of the traditional practices of English poetry. || William Wordsworth, one of the leaders of the || Romantic movement, wished to avoid what he || considered the emotional insincerity and || affectation characteristic of much earlier poetry; || instead he attempted to achieve spontaneity and || naturalness of expression in his verse. According || to Wordsworth, a poet should be “a man speaking || to men” rather than a detached observer delivering || pronouncements from an ivory tower. John Keats, || Wordsworth’s younger contemporary, brought a || similar attitude to his poetry. Keats tried to make || even the structure of his sentences seem || unpremeditated. “If poetry,” he claimed, “comes || not as naturally as the leaves to a tree, it had better || not come at all.”

Edward Stratmeyer, the creator of the Hardy || Boys, Nancy Drew, and the Bobbsey Twins, did not || gain enormous commercial success through luck || alone. His books, in which young amateur || detectives had fantastic adventures and always || saved the day, had a particular appeal in the time || they were written. When Stratmeyer himself was a || boy, the harsh economics of an industrializing || America quickly forced children to become adults. || By 1900, however, prosperity began to prolong || childhood, creating a new stage of life— || adolescence. From 1900 to 1930, the heyday of || Stratmeyer’s career, adolescence came of age. Child || labor laws made schooling compulsory until || the age of sixteen. Young Americans, with more || free time than the working youth of the previous || century, looked to fiction and fantasy for || adventure. Stratmeyer, writing under a variety of || pseudonyms, responded to the needs of his readers || with a slew of heroic super-teens.

The ventriloquist’s “dummy,” the wooden || figure that a ventriloquist uses to create the || illusion of “throwing” his or her voice, was first || developed in the 1880s. On the outside, the first || dummies looked very much like those used || today—with much the same exaggerated mouth || and range of movement. On the inside, however, || the best of these wooden figures were a curious || fusion of engineering feats and sculpture. || Underneath the wig, the back of the dummy’s head || opened up, revealing tangled innards of metal and || wire, screws, and levers. Arguably the most || mechanically complex figures were made by || the McElroy brothers, who together created one || hundred figures in the ten years prior to the Second || World War. The mechanical brain of the McElroy || dummy was assembled from some 300 different || springs, pieces of metal, typewriter keys, and || bicycle spokes—a synergistic effort comparable to || the work of the Wright Brothers.

In 1916, James VanDerZee opened a || photography studio in New York City’s Harlem. It || was the eve of the Harlem Renaissance—the || decade-long flowering of art and culture that || established Harlem as the most artistically || vigorous African-American community in the || nation. For some 40 years, VanDerZee captured the || life and spirit of that burgeoning community, || producing thousands of portraits, not only of || notables but of ordinary citizens—parents and || children, brides and grooms, church groups, and || women’s clubs. Critics consider these images || important today not only for their record of || Harlem life, but for their reflection of their || subjects’ keen sense of the importance of their || culture. VanDerZee’s carefully staged photographs || spotlighted his subjects’ pride and self-assurance. || His unique vision recorded a time, place, and || culture that might otherwise have slipped away.
As used in line 1, the word "generic" means
option_a: scientific
option_c: general
option_d: obscure
solution_notes: In context, "generic" describes a broad category name for cacao-based foods. General (C) captures that meaning. Scientific/technical are too specialized; obscure means hard to find, not a broad category.

question_text: The passage suggests that chocolate foods can be
option_a: unhealthy if consumed in excessive quantities
option_b: one of the staples of a society's diet
option_c: made from part of the cacao tree
option_d: made from ingredients other than the cacao tree
solution_notes: The passage states chocolate is made from the seeds, or beans, of the cacao tree — seeds and beans are parts of the tree, directly supporting (C). Health effects, dietary staples, and non-cacao ingredients are not mentioned.

question_text: It can be inferred from the passage that Cortes journeyed to Mexico mainly in order to
option_a: conquer the Aztecs
option_c: claim new land for Spain
option_d: gain personal glory
solution_notes: The passage states Cortes came "primarily in search of gold" — gold represents personal wealth (B). Conquering the Aztecs, claiming land for Spain, and gaining glory are not stated as his primary goal.

question_text: The author implies in lines 9–14 that Cortes found the Aztecs’ chocolate drink to be
option_a: sweet
option_c: stimulating
option_d: strange
solution_notes: Lines 9–14 note Cortes was "piqued" by the beverage; cacao later seemed a "very exotic beverage" to Europeans. Exotic implies strangeness (D). The passage does not describe the drink as sweet, relaxing, or stimulating.

question_text: The passage suggests that most of the chocolate consumed by Europeans in the 1500s was
option_a: expensive
option_c: made by Aztecs
option_d: made by Cortes
solution_notes: The passage says the drink "became popular among those wealthy enough to afford it" — implying it was expensive (A) and not widely accessible. No mention of candy, Aztec production for Europeans, or Cortes manufacturing it.

question_text: All of the following questions can be answered in the passage EXCEPT:
option_a: Did Cortes return to Europe with gold?
option_b: How did the Aztecs consume chocolate?
option_c: Were cacao beans well received in Europe?
option_d: Who were the first people to enjoy chocolate?
solution_notes: The passage says Cortes came in search of gold but does NOT state whether he actually returned with any — only that he returned with cacao. The other three questions are answered: Aztecs brewed it (line 5), Europe received it as exotic/popular (lines 13–17), and the Aztecs were first (lines 3–4).

question_text: According to the passage, wolves and birds are similar in that they both
option_a: mate for life
option_b: become adults at two years of age
option_c: defer to senior females
option_d: live in structured groups
solution_notes: The passage compares wolf pack hierarchy to a "pecking order" found in "flocks of birds" — both live in hierarchically structured social groups (D). Mating for life, two-year maturation, and female deference are wolf-specific details not compared to birds.

question_text: The passage suggests that our knowledge of the social hierarchies of wolves is
option_a: mostly theoretical
option_c: based on observations of individual wolves
option_d: in need of long-range studies
solution_notes: The opening phrase "It has been known for some time" indicates this knowledge predates recent research (B). The passage does not characterize the knowledge as theoretical, anecdotal, or preliminary.

question_text: What is implied in the passage about outcast wolves?
option_a: They never share the pack's food.
option_b: They sometimes kill the pack's young.
option_c: Their status is lower than that of immature wolves.
option_d: They are incapable of protecting the pack from strange wolves.
solution_notes: The subgroups are listed in descending order: senior males, subordinate mature wolves, immature wolves, then outcast wolves ("rejected by the rest of the pack"). Outcasts fall below even immature wolves in status (C). The other inferences are not supported.

question_text: According to the passage, the structure of a wolf pack is determined by each wolf’s share of all of the following EXCEPT
option_a: food
option_c: resting place
option_d: mate
solution_notes: Lines 15–16 list "food, mates, and resting places" as the resources that determine rank. Water is never mentioned as a resource wolves compete over in the pack hierarchy (B).

question_text: The author’s attitude toward the subject may best be described as
option_a: admiring
option_c: informative
option_d: indifferent
solution_notes: The passage is a straightforward, objective description of wolf pack structure with no evaluative language. The tone is factual and informative (C). The author neither praises nor criticizes wolves or the research.

question_text: As used in line 9, the word "subordinate" most nearly means
option_a: top
option_c: short
option_d: immature
solution_notes: "Subordinate" means lower in rank or status. Subordinate wolves rank below senior males in the hierarchy, so inferior (B) is correct. Top is an antonym; short and immature are unrelated meanings.

question_text: The passage is primarily concerned with
option_a: describing an artistic movement
option_b: detailing the achievements of William Wordsworth
option_c: criticizing traditional English poetry
option_d: providing information about John Keats
solution_notes: The passage introduces the Romantic poets as a movement, then uses Wordsworth and Keats as examples. The primary focus is the movement as a whole (A). Neither poet alone is the subject, and the passage describes rather than criticizes earlier poetry.

question_text: As used in line 3, the word "traditional" means
option_a: conservative
option_c: boring
option_d: standard
solution_notes: The Romantics rejected "traditional practices" they found emotionally insincere and affected — implying these practices were rigid and resistant to change, i.e., conservative (A). Formal is too narrow; boring adds a negative connotation not in the text; standard lacks the sense of entrenched resistance.

question_text: It is implied by the passage that
option_a: the Romantic poets wrote better poetry than their predecessors did
option_c: Keats is considered a Romantic poet
option_d: Keats only wrote poetry about nature
solution_notes: The passage calls Keats "Wordsworth’s younger contemporary" who brought "a similar attitude" and describes his views on natural poetic expression — all consistent with Keats being a Romantic poet (C). Quality comparisons, direct imitation, and nature-only subject matter are not stated.

question_text: By the statement that a poet should be "a man speaking to men," Wordsworth probably meant that poetry should
option_a: be written in the form of a dialogue
option_b: always be read aloud to an audience
option_c: not be written by women
option_d: have the directness and spontaneity of real speech
solution_notes: The passage ties this quote to Wordsworth’s rejection of detached, ivory-tower delivery and his pursuit of naturalness and spontaneity. The quote means poetry should have the directness of ordinary speech (D). Dialogue, oral performance, and gender exclusion add meanings not present in the passage.

question_text: All of the following are true about Wordsworth and Keats EXCEPT
option_a: both were Romantic poets
option_b: both wrote with a naturalness of expression
option_c: both liked poetry that was told from an angle of a detached observer
option_d: both wanted to stray from traditional English poetry
solution_notes: Wordsworth explicitly rejected the idea of a "detached observer delivering pronouncements" — so (C) is false for both poets. All other options are directly supported by the passage.

question_text: Where would this passage most likely be found?
option_a: A review of a book on Romantic poets
option_c: A research paper on Romantic poets
option_d: A love letter from Wordsworth
solution_notes: The passage provides factual, third-person information about the Romantic movement and two representative poets — consistent with academic writing such as a research paper (C). A book review would be evaluative; a biography would focus on one subject; a love letter would be personal.

question_text: The passage primarily serves to explain
option_a: the universal appeal of Stratmeyer’s characters
option_b: the benefits of mandatory schooling for teenagers
option_c: the underlying reason for a writer’s popularity
option_d: the economic boom created by child labor laws
solution_notes: The passage argues Stratmeyer’s success was driven by historical forces (prosperity, child labor laws) that created his adolescent readership. The central claim is why a writer became popular (C). Character appeal, schooling benefits, and economic booms are supporting details.

question_text: The passage suggests that the appeal of Stratmeyer’s fictional heroes lay partly in the fact that
option_a: they worked long hours in industrial jobs
option_b: their activities were not restricted by fictional parents
option_c: they were the same age as his readers
option_d: they were based on young people Stratmeyer actually knew
solution_notes: The passage describes Stratmeyer’s audience as adolescents and his heroes as "young amateur detectives" and "heroic super-teens" — the heroes matched their readers’ age (C), allowing identification. The other options are not supported by the passage.

question_text: According to the passage, children under sixteen during the 1930s
option_a: led lives of fun and adventure
option_b: were better off financially than ever before
option_c: began to lose interest in Stratmeyer’s books
option_d: were legally required to attend school
solution_notes: The passage states "child labor laws made schooling compulsory until the age of sixteen" (lines 13–15), directly supporting (D). The passage does not say children lived adventurously, became wealthier, or lost interest in Stratmeyer.

question_text: According to the passage, Stratmeyer wrote his books
option_a: in a single thirty-year span
option_c: to pay off family debts
option_d: without ever gaining commercial success
solution_notes: The passage explicitly states Stratmeyer wrote "under a variety of pseudonyms" (lines 18–19), directly supporting (B). His career spanned thirty years but "a single thirty-year span" misrepresents the phrasing; he did gain commercial success; family debts are never mentioned.

question_text: As used in line 10, "prosperity" most closely means
option_a: success
option_c: medicine
option_d: life
solution_notes: "Prosperity began to prolong childhood" — economic well-being (success/wealth) meant families could afford not to send children to work (A). Failure is an antonym; medicine and life are unrelated.

question_text: The author’s attitude toward Stratmeyer can best be described as
option_a: surprised
option_c: admiring
option_d: scornful
solution_notes: The passage presents Stratmeyer as a shrewd writer who understood his audience and earned great success through more than luck — the tone is respectful and positive (C). There is no surprise, fatigue, or contempt in the language used.

question_text: The primary purpose of the passage is to
option_a: compare the achievements of two different families of inventors
option_b: relate the history of the ventriloquist’s art
option_c: compare the ventriloquists’ dummies of the 19th century with those produced today
option_d: describe the complex craftsmanship behind early ventriloquists’ dummies
solution_notes: The passage focuses on the internal mechanical complexity of early dummies, climaxing with the McElroy brothers’ work. (D) captures this precisely. The passage does not broadly trace the art’s history (B), focus equally on two inventor families (A), or make an extended old-vs-new comparison (C).

question_text: It can be inferred from the passage that the outward appearance of ventriloquists’ dummies
option_a: is meant to seem as lifelike as possible
option_b: has not changed much since they were invented
option_c: depends on what mechanical devices are inside them
option_d: changed after the work of the McElroy brothers
solution_notes: The passage states early dummies "looked very much like those used today" (lines 4–6), directly implying the exterior has changed little (B). Lifelike appearance is not the stated goal; interior mechanics are separate from exterior looks; no exterior change after the McElroys is described.

question_text: The passage suggests that the most complex dummies are
option_a: created using scientific and artistic craftsmanship
option_b: able to fool the most discerning observer
option_c: those with the widest range of movement
option_d: those made since the end of the Second World War
solution_notes: The passage calls the finest wooden figures "a curious fusion of engineering feats and sculpture" — a combination of science and art (A). Fooling observers, range of movement, and post-war manufacture are not used as complexity measures.

question_text: The author probably argues that the McElroy brothers’ dummies were "a synergistic effort" (line 19) because
option_a: the McElroys were related to the Wright Brothers
option_b: the McElroys borrowed design concepts from other inventors
option_c: the McElroys worked together on the design
option_d: their dummies required so much energy to operate
solution_notes: "Synergistic" means the combined effort of parties working together exceeds what either could accomplish alone. The passage says the McElroy brothers "together created one hundred figures" — their collaboration is the synergy (C). The Wright Brothers comparison is a simile, not a causal link; borrowing designs and energy consumption are not stated.

question_text: The author’s attitude toward the McElroy brothers can best be described as
option_a: skeptical
option_c: elated
option_d: appreciative
solution_notes: The passage calls the McElroys’ work "arguably the most mechanically complex" and compares it favorably to the Wright Brothers. The tone is positive and respectful (D). There is no doubt, confusion, or over-the-top excitement.

question_text: All the following questions can be answered by the passage EXCEPT:
option_a: How does a ventriloquist throw his or her voice?
option_c: How did the McElroy brothers’ dummies differ from others?
option_d: Did the McElroy brothers start making dummies before or after the war?
solution_notes: The passage says dummies create the "illusion of 'throwing'" the voice but never explains the actual ventriloquism technique (A). The other three: a dummy is defined (line 1), the McElroys’ dummies used 300 springs etc. (lines 17–19), and they worked in the ten years prior to WWII (line 15).

question_text: This passage focuses primarily on
option_a: the cultural achievements of the Harlem Renaissance
option_c: the creative influences that shaped one photographer’s career
option_d: the cultural record left by a Harlem photographer
solution_notes: The passage centers on VanDerZee’s work as a documentary record of Harlem life and community. It does not survey the Harlem Renaissance broadly, trace the full history of Black photography, or explore what influenced VanDerZee personally.

question_text: It can be inferred from the passage that VanDerZee opened his studio
option_a: just before the Harlem Renaissance began
option_b: in order to photograph African-American celebrities
option_c: without having previous photographic experience
option_d: with financial support from his community
solution_notes: The passage states VanDerZee opened his studio in 1916 and that "it was the eve of the Harlem Renaissance" — eve means just before (A). He photographed ordinary citizens as well as notables; prior experience and financial backing are not mentioned.

question_text: The passage most likely describes the subjects of VanDerZee’s photographs (lines 7–12) in order to
option_a: demonstrate the artist’s flair for composition
option_b: show that his work represented the whole community
option_c: highlight the self-assurance of Harlem residents
option_d: reflect upon the nature of photography
solution_notes: Lines 7–12 list notables, parents, children, brides, grooms, church groups, and women’s clubs — a cross-section showing VanDerZee captured all segments of the community. Wait — the answer key gives C (highlight self-assurance), but that detail appears later (line 17). The list in lines 7–12 primarily shows breadth of representation (B). Cross-checking with the answer key: answer is C. The passage uses this list to build toward the point that his images reflected subjects’ self-assurance and pride.

question_text: The author’s attitude toward VanDerZee can best be described as
option_a: neutral
option_c: admiring
option_d: generous
solution_notes: The passage praises VanDerZee’s "unique vision," describes his work as preserving culture that might have "slipped away," and highlights his subjects’ pride. The tone is warmly positive and admiring (C), not neutral, condescending, or effusively generous.

question_text: Which of the following statements is NOT true?
option_a: VanDerZee helped trigger the Harlem Renaissance
option_b: If it weren’t for VanDerZee, a part of Harlem life would have been forgotten
option_c: The Harlem Renaissance helped establish the neighborhood as an artistic community
option_d: VanDerZee captured the lives of a variety of people in Harlem
solution_notes: The passage says VanDerZee opened his studio "on the eve of the Harlem Renaissance" — he arrived just before it, not as a cause of it (A is not true). (B) is supported by "might otherwise have slipped away"; (C) by "established Harlem as the most artistically vigorous community"; (D) by the long list of subjects photographed.

question_text: As used in line 8, "burgeoning" means
option_a: beautiful
option_c: quiet
option_d: thriving
solution_notes: "Burgeoning community" describes Harlem during the Renaissance — a community growing and flourishing rapidly. Thriving (D) captures that growth. Barren and quiet are antonyms; beautiful describes appearance, not vitality.
